lessons.title: What bots can and can't do
lessons.body_md:
# What bots can and can't do

Trading bots are sold with big promises. Let's be precise about what automation actually changes — and what it doesn't.

## What a bot is

A bot is a program that, on a schedule (say every hourly close), reads market data, applies fixed rules, and — if allowed — places orders through an exchange API. OMEGA's bots work exactly like this: *"at every hourly close, fetch closed candles, run every rule in approved.json whose status allows the mode, and (testnet/live) place the orders on Binance USDT-M futures with a protective stop, cancel unfilled limits when the rule's window ends, and sell when the rule's hold time is over."*

## What bots are good at

1. **Consistency.** They take every valid setup and skip every invalid one. No FOMO, no revenge, no hesitation.
2. **Speed and coverage.** They can scan hundreds of coins every hour — useful for rare setups like the panic bounce, which needs many coins to find enough fills.
3. **Unsocial hours.** Crypto panics happen at 3 a.m. Bots don't sleep.
4. **Exact rules.** The same code can run in backtest, paper and live. OMEGA's design: *"a live signal is trade-for-trade the backtest's."* That makes the forward record directly comparable with the test.
5. **Enforcing limits.** A guard can refuse oversized orders, cap leverage, and stop trading at a daily loss limit — reliably.

## What bots cannot do

1. **Create an edge.** A bot running a rule with no edge loses money faster and more consistently than a human. CREED automated is still −0.10R to −0.12R a trade.
2. **Adapt intelligently.** A bot doesn't know the market has changed. Fading edges keep being traded until *you* stop them.
3. **Avoid technical risk.** Bugs, internet outages, exchange API changes, rate limits, wrong settings, a key with too many permissions.
4. **Guarantee fills.** Real fills differ from backtests; slippage, partial fills and rejected orders happen.
5. **Protect you from the tails.** A bot following a fat-tailed rule will take the −80% trade just as faithfully as the +20% one.

## Bots and the evidence

Look at the OMEGA bot page: *"PAPER TRADING. No real orders are placed by any bot on this page. None of them is connected to a broker. Every bot trades simulated positions against real prices and records the results as simulated."* Some bots in the Journal are marked *retired*.

And the separate trading-bot system for Binance only allows rules listed in `approved.json` — the spec says *"anything else is refused"* — and each rule's `max_leverage` is the highest leverage the research showed with no liquidations (**1**).

## Typical bot marketing claims — and the reality

| Claim | Reality |
|---|---|
| "90% win rate" | Win rate says nothing about expectancy; high win rates often hide big losers |
| "1% a day" | That's over 3,600% a year compounded. OMEGA's Monte Carlo: no strategy turned 100 into 1,000,000 in 5 years |
| "AI-powered" | OMEGA's neural network (E32) and ML scouts (E81/E82) found little tradeable direction after costs |
| "Backtested returns of 500%" | Ask: out of sample? after costs? including delisted coins? how many variants tried? |
| "Set and forget" | Edges fade; bots need monitoring, kill switches and retirement rules |

## When automation makes sense

- You have a **rule tested fairly** (or you're running a paper/testnet experiment to build a forward record).
- The rule is **exact** — no judgement calls.
- Human execution would be **impractical** (many coins, odd hours).
- You have **guards, a kill switch and small size**.

## Exercise

1. Open the **Trading Bots** page in OMEGA and the **Bot control room**. Confirm that everything is paper and note where results are recorded.
2. Find one bot advert or social-media claim. Write the five questions from the table you would ask before believing it.
3. Open **Autopilot** and read what it does: researches, tests and paper-trades while the app is open, *never real orders*.
key_points: Bots apply fixed rules on a schedule; OMEGA's same code runs in backtest, paper and live.
Bots are good at consistency, coverage, odd hours, exact rules and enforcing limits.
Bots can't create an edge, adapt to fading markets, avoid technical risk or escape fat tails.
OMEGA's app bots are paper only; the Binance bot trades only rules in approved.json, at max 1× leverage.
Question every bot claim: out of sample, after costs, delisted coins, number of variants.

quiz.q: What happens if you automate a rule with no edge?
options: It loses money consistently and quickly
quiz.why: Automation executes the rule faithfully, including its negative expectancy.

quiz.q: Why is OMEGA's 'same code in backtest, paper and live' design valuable?
options: Live signals match the backtest trade for trade, so forward records are comparable
quiz.why: Comparing like with like is how you judge whether the edge still works.

quiz.q: A bot advertises '1% a day'. What's the right reaction?
options: Use 20× to make it 20% a day
Sceptical: it implies extreme compounding; the research found nothing close
quiz.why: No strategy in the Monte Carlo turned 100 into 1,000,000 in 5 years.

quiz.q: What does the Binance bot do with a rule not listed in approved.json?
quiz.why: approved.json is the list the bot is allowed to trade; anything else is refused.

lessons.title: 'Small win every day' bots and their blow-ups
lessons.body_md:
# "Small win every day" bots and their blow-ups

Some bot strategies produce beautiful, smooth equity curves — until they don't. Understanding why will protect you from the most common way automated accounts are wiped out.

## The shape of the problem

```
Equity
  |                         ___/‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾\
  |               ___/‾‾‾‾‾              \
  |      ___/‾‾‾‾                          \
  | ___/                                    \____
  +------------------------------------------------ time
     months of small, steady wins       one event
```

These strategies **sell insurance**: they collect small payments most of the time and pay out a large amount occasionally. The expected value can be negative even though most days are green.

## Common examples

### Grid bots
Place buy orders below and sell orders above the price at fixed intervals. In a range, they buy low and sell high repeatedly. In a strong trend down, they keep buying all the way, ending with a large position far underwater. With leverage, that ends in liquidation.

### Martingale / averaging down
Double the size after each loss so one win recovers everything. Works until a long losing streak (which always comes, Module 5) requires a size the account can't afford.

```
Start 1 USDT, double after each loss:
Losses: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 → 8 losses = 255 USDT lost
The 9th trade must be 256 USDT to win back... 1 USDT
```

### Funding harvest (delta-neutral carry)
Buy spot, short the perp, collect funding. OMEGA tested this (E34): **+8.8% a year in 2021–24, then −17% a year in 2025–26, including one funding flip that lost −64.6% in a single month.**

### High-win-rate scalpers
Tight target, wide (or no) stop. Win 90% of trades, lose ten times the average win on the rest. Expectancy ≈ 0.9 × 1 − 0.1 × 10 = −0.1 per unit — before costs.

### Market-neutral books with short legs
OMEGA's cross-sectional test (E52): in April 2026 the short leg held a coin that rose about **50× in a week**, and **the book lost more than 100% in a day**. Shorting small coins carries squeeze-ruin risk.

## Why they're attractive

- They match the wish for steady daily income (Module 8, psychology).
- Short backtests or live periods rarely include the blow-up, so they look safe.
- High win rates feel like skill.

## How to spot one

Ask these questions about any bot or strategy:

1. **What's the worst single trade or day** in the full history? Not the average.
2. **What happens in a 30–50% crash** or a 50% spike in one day?
3. **Does it add to losing positions?** (grids, martingale, averaging down)
4. **Is the stop much wider than the target?**
5. **Does the history include 2021's boom, 2022's crashes and the October 2025 wick** (a −83% intrabar move was recorded)?
6. **Is there leverage?** Leverage turns a bad day into liquidation.

## The research's summary

OMEGA's main lessons include: *"'small win every day' strategies (grids, funding harvest, high-win-rate bots) carry rare blow-ups."* And for the funding book, the app's own monitor warns that carry *"can flip negative in selloffs, and holds exchange counterparty risk"*.

## The honest alternative

The setups that actually passed are the opposite shape: **many small losses or flat periods, occasional big wins** (the edge lives in the big rebounds). That shape is psychologically harder but doesn't hide a cliff — as long as positions are small and unleveraged.

## Worked example: a grid at 5×

```
Account 100 USDT. Grid buys 10 USDT notional every 2% down, 5× leverage (2 USDT margin each).
Price falls 20%: 10 buys = 100 USDT notional, average entry about 11% below the start.
  Unrealised loss ≈ 100 × (0.89 − 0.80) / 0.89 ≈ 10 USDT. Uncomfortable, survivable.
Price falls 40%: 20 buys = 200 USDT notional (40 USDT margin), average entry about −21%.
  Unrealised loss ≈ 200 × (0.79 − 0.60) / 0.79 ≈ 48 USDT.
Price falls 60% (it happens in crypto): 30 buys = 300 USDT notional, loss ≈ 126 USDT
  → more than the whole account: liquidated well before this point.
```

The grid "won" every small wiggle for months, then one crash took the account.

## Exercise

1. Open the **Simulation** page and read the funding-rate carry monitor and its warning text.
2. Take any bot strategy you've heard of and answer the six questions above.
3. Write a rule in your plan: "I will not run strategies that add to losing positions or that have a stop more than __× the target."
key_points: 'Small win every day' strategies sell insurance: steady small gains, rare huge losses.
Grids, martingale, funding harvests, high-win-rate scalpers and short-leg books share this shape.
Funding harvest (E34): +8.8%/yr 2021–24, then −17%/yr with a −64.6% month; E52's short leg lost >100% in a day.
Judge strategies by worst trade and worst day, crash behaviour, averaging down and stop-to-target ratio.
The passed setups have the opposite shape — but only small, unleveraged positions keep that safe.

quiz.q: Martingale starting at 1 USDT loses 8 in a row. How much has been lost?
A scalper wins 90% at +1 and loses 10% at −10. Expectancy before costs?
What happened in E52's cross-sectional book in April 2026?
options: A short leg rose about 50× in a week and the book lost over 100% in a day
quiz.why: Short legs on small coins carry squeeze-ruin risk.

quiz.q: Which question best reveals a hidden blow-up risk?
options: What's the worst single trade or day in the full history?
quiz.why: Averages and win rates hide tails; worst outcomes show them.

lessons.title: Paper → testnet → live: the ladder
lessons.body_md:
# Paper → testnet → live

Every automated strategy should climb a ladder, one rung at a time. Each rung tests something different. Skipping rungs is how bugs and bad ideas meet real money.

## Rung 1 — Backtest

**Tests:** the idea, on history, with costs. (Module 7.)
**Doesn't test:** your code in real time, fills, exchange behaviour.

OMEGA's bots have a backtest command that uses the same strategy code, for example:

```
python -m edges.bots backtest --strategy panic_h1 --from 2024-01-01
```

## Rung 2 — Paper

**Tests:** that the bot runs reliably in real time, produces the signals you expect, logs correctly, and that the forward results look like the backtest's.
**Doesn't test:** real order handling, real fills.

OMEGA: *"Paper first (no keys): double-click run_paper.bat. It runs forever; every signal, order, fill and exit is written to bots_log.jsonl and the state to state.json."* A `status` command shows open positions and the last log lines. Recommended: **a few days at least**, and ideally many trades.

## Rung 3 — Testnet

**Tests:** real order mechanics against a demo exchange — placing orders, protective stops, cancelling unfilled limits, closing at hold time, handling errors.
**Doesn't test:** real liquidity and real prices.

OMEGA's instructions for Binance's futures testnet:

- Create a **testnet API key** and store it with `setkey testnet` — it goes into the operating system's credential vault, *never a file*.
- Set the rule's status to `testnet` in `approved.json`.
- The account must be in **One-way Mode**.
- *"Testnet prices differ from the real market: signals come from real candles and limit prices are re-based by the testnet/real price ratio."*

## Rung 4 — Live (tiny)

**Tests:** everything, with real money at stake.

OMEGA's live switch is deliberately hard. **All** of these are required, and *"any one missing = refused"*:

1. **50+ testnet trades that look like the backtest.**
2. A real API key with **futures only, no withdrawals, restricted to your IP**, stored with `setkey live`.
3. `"status": "live"` for that rule in `approved.json` — *"only the owner sets this by hand"*.
4. `"live": true` in the config file.
5. An environment variable typed in the terminal: `OMEGA_LIVE=I_UNDERSTAND_REAL_MONEY`.

That friction is intentional. Going live should be a calm, deliberate decision, never a click.

## What to compare at each rung

| Check | Paper | Testnet | Live |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signals match backtest for the same period | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Orders placed / cancelled correctly | — | ✓ | ✓ |
| Stops placed on every position | — | ✓ | ✓ |
| Fill prices vs assumed | — | partly | ✓ |
| Average result per trade vs backtest | rough | rough | ✓ (after many trades) |

## How long on each rung?

- **Paper:** until you've seen the bot run through restarts, quiet periods and at least a few signals.
- **Testnet:** 50+ trades, per OMEGA's rule.
- **Live:** start with the minimum size and keep it there for at least 100 trades before considering any change.

For rare setups (the climax fires only occasionally), this takes months. That's fine. There's no deadline.

## Honest limits

OMEGA's bot README is candid: exchange calls were tested against a **simulated Binance** only, because the research environment couldn't reach the real exchange or testnet; the bots had *"never run on Windows, against the real testnet, or with MetaTrader 5"* at that time. That is exactly why the ladder exists — each rung finds problems the previous one couldn't.

## Exercise

1. Write the ladder for one strategy you'd consider automating: what you'll check at each rung, and the minimum number of trades or days before moving up.
2. If you have the OMEGA bots, run paper mode and use `status` to view positions and the log. Note one thing that surprised you.
3. Write your personal "go live" checklist with the five OMEGA conditions plus any of your own.
key_points: Each rung tests something different: backtest (idea), paper (real-time running), testnet (order mechanics), live (everything).
Paper first with no keys; every signal, order, fill and exit is logged.
Testnet keys go in the OS credential vault; testnet prices differ, so it tests mechanics more than profit.
Live requires 50+ matching testnet trades, a no-withdrawal IP-restricted key, and several manual switches.
Rare setups take months to climb the ladder — there's no deadline.

options: Leverage limits on the real market
Real order mechanics: placement, stops, cancellations, errors
quiz.why: Testnet prices differ from the real market, so it's a mechanics test.

quiz.q: Which API key setting is required for OMEGA's live mode?
options: Futures only, no withdrawals, restricted to your IP
quiz.why: A minimal-permission key limits the damage if it's ever leaked.

quiz.q: How many matching testnet trades does OMEGA require before live?
quiz.why: Go live only if 50+ testnet trades look like the backtest.

quiz.q: Why is OMEGA's live switch deliberately hard to turn on?
options: To make going live a calm, deliberate decision, not a click
quiz.why: Multiple manual steps prevent accidental or impulsive live trading.

lessons.title: Guards, kill switches and key safety
lessons.body_md:
# Guards, kill switches and key safety

A bot will do exactly what it's told, very fast, forever. Guards limit what it *can* do when something goes wrong — a bug, a bad signal, a market crash, or a mistake in settings.

## OMEGA's guard (config.json → guard)

| Guard | Setting | What it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| Hard leverage cap | **3×**, and each rule's `max_leverage` (now **1×**) | Accidental high leverage |
| Margin per order | **≤ 10 USDT** | One oversized order |
| Open positions / resting entries | **≤ 3**, counted **from the exchange**, not only the bot's file | Runaway order loops; state-file errors |
| Positions per coin | **One** | Doubling up by accident |
| Risk per trade (size × stop) | **≤ 3 USDT** | Large single losses |
| Daily loss limit | **5 USDT** | A bad day spiralling |
| Stop on every position | Inside the liquidation distance, **2% buffer live** | Liquidation before the stop |
| Stop can't be placed | **Entry undone**; if that fails too, **kill switch** and the position is marked UNPROTECTED and closed | Naked positions |

Notice the design: limits are checked against the **exchange**, not just the bot's memory. If the bot's state file is wrong, the exchange is the source of truth.

## The kill switch

> *"KILL_all.bat (or python -m edges.bots kill) cancels every order, closes every position on the futures account and blocks new orders."*

It also writes the OMEGA Bridge's KILL file, and the bots obey the Bridge's kill too — *one switch for both*. `kill_off` lifts it.

Every automated setup you run should have:

1. **One action that stops everything** — cancels orders, closes positions, blocks new ones.
2. **Easy access** — a desktop shortcut, a phone action, or a written procedure.
3. **A test** — try it on paper/testnet so you know it works before you need it.

## When to press it

- The bot is placing orders you don't understand.
- Positions exist without stops.
- The exchange or your internet is behaving strangely.
- A major market event (exchange hack, extreme crash) and you're unsure.
- The daily loss limit is hit but orders keep coming.

Pressing the kill switch "too early" costs little. Pressing it too late can cost the account.

## API key safety

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **No withdrawal permission, ever** | A leaked key can then trade badly but can't send your funds away |
| **Futures only** (or only what the bot needs) | Least privilege |
| **Restrict to your IP address** | A stolen key won't work from elsewhere |
| **Store in the OS vault or environment variables** | OMEGA refuses config files containing a key/secret and redacts secrets in logs |
| **Separate keys for testnet and live** | No mix-ups |
| **Use a sub-account with limited funds** | The bot can only lose what's in it |
| **Rotate keys** if you suspect anything | Cheap insurance |

## Account-level protections

- **Isolated margin** so one position can't drain the wallet.
- **Small balance on the bot account** — keep the rest elsewhere.
- **2FA** on the exchange account; withdrawal address whitelisting.

## Guards for manual trading too

The same ideas apply to you:

- Risk Guard limits (0.5% a trade, 2 open, −2% day, −5% week).
- Stop on every position, placed at entry.
- A "kill switch" habit: when in doubt, flatten and step away.

## Worked example: a guard saving the day

```
Bug: a strategy sends a long signal on every coin at once (a data glitch).
Without guard: 40 orders × 10 USDT = 400 USDT notional on a 100 USDT account.
With guard: ≤ 3 open positions counted from the exchange → 3 orders accepted,
            37 refused; risk per trade ≤ 3 USDT; daily loss limit 5 USDT.
Worst case: about 5 USDT, then trading stops. Owner presses KILL, investigates.
```

## Exercise

1. Write a guard config for any bot you might run: leverage cap, margin per order, max open, risk per trade, daily loss limit.
2. Find the kill switch for your setup (OMEGA's KILL_all, or your exchange's "close all") and practise it on paper or testnet.
3. Check every API key you own: remove withdrawal permission and add IP restrictions where possible.
key_points: OMEGA's guard: 3× hard cap (rules at 1×), ≤10 USDT margin per order, ≤3 open (counted from the exchange), ≤3 USDT risk, 5 USDT daily loss.
Every position needs a stop inside the liquidation distance; if a stop can't be placed, the entry is undone.
Have one tested kill switch that cancels orders, closes positions and blocks new ones.
API keys: no withdrawals, minimal permissions, IP-restricted, stored in the OS vault, never in files.
Use isolated margin and a small sub-account balance for bots.

options: The exchange is the source of truth if the bot's state file is wrong
quiz.why: State files can be out of date; the exchange shows real exposure.

quiz.q: What does OMEGA's kill switch do?
options: Cancels every order, closes every position and blocks new orders
quiz.why: It's a single action to stop everything.

quiz.q: Which API key permission should a trading bot never have?
quiz.why: Without withdrawal permission a leaked key can't move funds out.

quiz.q: What happens in OMEGA's bots if a protective stop can't be placed?
options: The entry is undone; if that fails, kill switch and close
quiz.why: No position is allowed to stay naked.

lessons.title: Reading a forward record
lessons.body_md:
# Reading a forward record

A **forward record** is a list of trades or predictions made in real time, recorded as they happened, and never edited. It's the most honest evidence there is — if you know how to read it.

## Why forward records matter

Backtests can be wrong in many ways (Module 7). A forward record can't be overfitted to data that didn't exist yet. That's why OMEGA's research says the passed setups need *"the forward-ticket record ... before trusting them with money"*, and why the scouts run live as *"public, forward-scored predictions"* that *"feed no bot until their forward record shows skill"*.

## What a trustworthy forward record looks like

1. **Timestamped before the outcome.** Signals are published or logged when made.
2. **Complete.** Every signal, including losers and ones not traded. OMEGA Signals: *"Every signal is followed to its outcome and recorded in the Journal."*
3. **Unedited.** No deleting, no "that one doesn't count".
4. **Same rules as tested.** OMEGA Signals' *"stop, target and 24-hour limit are exactly the terms the Lab tested"*; the bots' live code is the backtest code.
5. **After real costs.**
6. **Compared with a baseline.** The Scoreboard judges each product against *"a system with no skill at the same reward:risk"*.

## Five questions to ask

### 1. How many trades?
Small records mean almost nothing. Using the standard error formula from Module 5:

```
SD of results 1.3R:
  30 trades: SE = 1.3 / 5.5 ≈ 0.24R → an average of +0.2R is within noise
  100 trades: SE = 0.13R
  300 trades: SE = 0.075R
```

For fat-tailed setups like the panic bounce (single trades from −90% to big rebounds), you need **hundreds**.

### 2. How does it compare with the backtest?
If the backtest said +0.2% a trade and the forward record after 200 trades is −0.1%, something is different: costs, fills, market change, or the edge was never real.

### 3. Without the best few trades?
Does the result depend on one or two huge winners? (H1 loses without its best 5% — so a forward record of H1 might look negative for long stretches even if the edge is still there.)

### 4. Worst trade, worst day, max drawdown?
Do they fit what the test said? A worst trade far beyond the test's range is a red flag.

### 5. Against a no-skill baseline?
For a 2:1 reward:risk system, a no-skill trader wins about a third of the time. A 35% win rate at 2:1 isn't skill; it's roughly the baseline minus costs.

## Worked example: judging a signal record

```
Signal service: 60 trades, win rate 58%, average +0.35R after costs
SD per trade: 1.2R
SE = 1.2 / √60 = 1.2 / 7.75 = 0.155R
t = 0.35 / 0.155 ≈ 2.26
```

Promising — **if** the record is complete, unedited and pre-timestamped, and **if** it isn't the best of many services or periods shown to you (survivorship again: you rarely see the services that failed). Next steps: keep watching for 100–200 more trades; check the worst trades; compare with the stated rules.

## Red flags in forward records

- Screenshots of wins, no complete list.
- Records that start "from our best month".
- Results shown only as % of account with unknown leverage.
- Signals deleted or "updated" after the fact.
- No costs, or "before fees".
- A record shorter than the strategy's typical drawdown.

## Building your own forward record

Everything in this course points here. Whether manual or automated:

1. Write the rules (Module 7).
2. Log every signal and trade in the Journal, real and simulated separate.
3. Compare monthly with the test and a baseline.
4. Apply your retirement rule.

## Exercise

1. Open **OMEGA Signals** → *Live results against the research*. Note the number of closed signals and how they compare with the research.
2. Open the **Scoreboard** and read *"Same period, side by side"*. Is either product clearly above the no-skill line? With how many trades?
3. Take any public trading record you can find and score it against the six "trustworthy" criteria and the red-flag list.
key_points: A forward record is timestamped before outcomes, complete, unedited, uses the tested rules and includes costs.
Judge it by number of trades, comparison with the backtest, dependence on best trades, worst outcomes and a no-skill baseline.
Small records mean little; fat-tailed setups need hundreds of trades.
OMEGA Signals use exactly the Lab's tested terms and are followed to outcome; the Scoreboard compares against no-skill.
Red flags: screenshots only, cherry-picked start dates, unknown leverage, edits, no costs.

quiz.q: Which makes a forward record trustworthy?
options: Complete, unedited, timestamped before outcomes, after costs
quiz.why: Completeness and pre-timestamping are what make it honest.

quiz.q: 60 trades, average +0.35R, SD 1.2R. Roughly what is t?
For a 2:1 reward:risk system, what is a no-skill win rate (roughly)?
quiz.why: Break-even at 2:1 is 1/(1+2) ≈ 33%.

quiz.q: Why might an H1 forward record look negative for long stretches even if the edge still exists?
options: Because H1 loses without its best 5% of trades, which are rare
quiz.why: Results depend on rare big rebounds, so long flat or losing spells are expected.

lessons.body_md:
# Why a written trading plan

A trading plan is a short document that answers, in advance, every question you would otherwise answer emotionally in the middle of a trade. Professionals have one. Most losing retail traders don't.

## What a plan does for you

1. **Makes decisions before emotions.** The plan was written calmly; the market won't be calm.
2. **Defines your edge — or admits you don't have one yet.** "I'm practising and building a forward record" is an honest, valid plan.
3. **Sets your risk** so one bad day can't end your trading.
4. **Makes review possible.** You can only measure "did I follow the plan?" if there is a plan.
5. **Protects you from shiny new ideas.** Any new idea must go through testing (Module 7) before it enters the plan.

## The sections of a plan

| Section | Questions it answers | Module |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Purpose and goals | Why am I trading? What does success look like this year (in process, not money)? | 1 |
| 2. Capital and products | How much money (that I can afford to lose)? Spot, perps, CFDs? Which exchange/broker? | 2 |
| 3. Markets and schedule | Which 2–3 markets? Which hours (T&T time)? News rules? | 3, 8 |
| 4. Setups | Exactly which setups, with what evidence? Entry, stop, exit rules | 4, 6, 7 |
| 5. Risk rules | Risk per trade, max open, daily/weekly stops, leverage, review level | 5 |
| 6. Execution | Order types, alerts, when orders are placed, stops at entry | 2 |
| 7. Routine | Pre-market checklist, trading window, end-of-day | 8 |
| 8. Records and review | Journal fields, weekly and monthly reviews | 8 |
| 9. Testing and retirement | How new ideas are tested; when a setup is retired | 6, 7 |
| 10. Automation (optional) | Which bots, which rung of the ladder, guards, kill switch | 9 |
| 11. Personal rules | Stop-trading list, tilt signs, what I do after a limit is hit | 8 |

## Principles for writing it

- **Short.** Two pages is better than twenty. You must be able to read it before every session.
- **Specific.** Numbers, times and exact rules — not "be disciplined".
- **Honest about evidence.** For each setup, write what evidence it has (tested by me? by OMEGA? untested?) and what its expected result is.
- **Conservative.** Start with the Risk Guard defaults or smaller.
- **Versioned.** Date it. Change it only at reviews, never during a trading session.

## Goals: process, not profit

Profit goals ("make 10% a month") push you to over-trade and over-size. The research shows how unpredictable results are — even the passed setups had long losing stretches and years with most of the profit in one year. Set **process goals** instead:

- "Follow my pre-market checklist on 90% of trading days."
- "Log 100% of trades with all fields."
- "Zero trades above my risk limit this month."
- "Complete 100 paper trades of my setup and a full review."

## Evidence labels for setups

Use a simple label for each setup in your plan:

| Label | Meaning | Allowed size |
|---|---|---|
| **Tested-pass** | Passed your own fair test or OMEGA's, forward record building | Minimum live size (after paper/testnet) |
| **Watch** | Promising (grade C, or partial test) | Paper only |
| **Untested** | No fair test yet | Paper only |
| **Failed / retired** | Failed a test or its retirement rule | None |

By these labels, CREED is "Failed" as an edge (but may be used as a discipline checklist), the climax and panic bounce are "Tested-pass, fading", E66 and E68-F6 are "Watch", and most indicator rules are "Untested" until you test them.

## Exercise

1. Write section 1 of your plan now: why you trade (look back at your sentence from Module 1), and three process goals for the next month.
2. List every setup you currently use or want to use, and give each an evidence label.
3. Open the **Risk Guard** page and copy its rules into a draft section 5.

## A worked example

```
TRADING PLAN — version 1   Date 2026-11-15

1. PURPOSE AND GOALS
   Why: build a skill and a second income over years, not weeks.
   Goals: (a) checklist on 90% of trading days; (b) journal 100% of trades
          incl. emotion; (c) 0 trades above 0.5% risk.

2. CAPITAL AND PRODUCTS
   Capital: 300 USDT on Binance (sub-account) + 200 USD on Exness. Money I can lose.
   Products: Binance USDT-M perps, ISOLATED margin, 1×. Exness CFDs, smallest lots.

3. MARKETS AND SCHEDULE
   Markets: BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, XAUUSD.
   Window: 19:30–21:30 T&T weekdays (after work). Gold only if a setup
           is still valid from my morning check. No new trades after 21:30.
   News: flat or no new entries 30 min before/after US CPI, jobs, FOMC.
   Not trading: Fridays after a losing week; any day I'm tired or upset.

4. SETUPS
   A) Climax reversal (OMEGA, grade A, fading)
      Label: Tested-pass, fading → PAPER via OMEGA Signals/bots until 50 forward trades.
      Rules exactly as tested: 3σ hourly drop, 3× volume, close top 40%;
      buy next open, exit 12 h. Expected: ~+1% a trade 2025–26 but t < 1.
      Retire: if 100 forward trades average below 0.
   B) Structured pullback (CREED checklist)
      Label: Failed as an edge (−0.10 to −0.12R). Used only as a discipline
      exercise at 0.25% risk, max 2 a week. Stop if 50 trades average below −0.1R.
   C) My idea: gold London-open fade
      Label: Untested → test plan written 2026-11-10; paper only.

5. RISK RULES
   Risk/trade 0.5% (0.25% for B). Max open 2 (BTC+ETH same side = 1).
   Daily stop −2% or 3 losses. Weekly stop −5%. Review at −20% from peak.
   Max leverage 1× on perps. Stop inside liquidation distance always.

6. EXECUTION
   Limit entries where tested; stop-market, reduce-only, placed with the entry.
   Alerts at levels; no screen-watching.

7. ROUTINE
   19:00–19:25 checklist (Market Read, Signals, CREED, Risk Guard, calendar).
   End: journal + 5-minute note.

8. RECORDS AND REVIEW
   OMEGA Journal; real and simulated separate. Weekly: Saturday 09:00.
   Monthly: first Sunday — expectancy, drawdown, retirement rules.

9. TESTING NEW IDEAS
   Plan first; discovery/validation/final; luck check vs random entries;
   pass = final > 0 after costs, t ≥ 2, ≥ 100 trades. Then paper 50.

10. AUTOMATION
   OMEGA paper bot for setup A. Testnet only after 50 paper trades.
   Guard: 1×, ≤10 USDT margin, ≤3 open, daily loss 5 USDT. Kill switch on desktop.

11. PERSONAL RULES
   Stop-trading list: tired, angry, after 3 losses, after a big win, during news.
   Tilt signs: checking P&L constantly, switching to 5m. Response: close app 30 min.
   After a limit: journal, no trading until next session, first trade half size.
```

## Sanity checks for your plan

```
[ ] Could a stranger follow my setup rules exactly?
[ ] Is every setup labelled with its evidence?
[ ] Is my maximum daily loss a number in currency?
[ ] Is leverage limited to what tests showed survives (1× for everything tested here)?
[ ] Does the schedule fit my real life?
[ ] Is there a retirement rule for each setup?
[ ] Is there a kill switch / stop-trading rule?
```

## Exercise

1. Fill in the full template for yourself. Keep it to two pages.
2. Run it through the sanity checks.
3. Save it with a version number and date. Print it or keep it open next to OMEGA.

# A 30-day practice schedule

Knowledge becomes skill through repetition. This schedule turns the course into 30 days of practice — about 30–60 minutes a day — using the OMEGA app and paper trading. No real money is required.

## Week 1 — Mechanics and mark-ups (days 1–7)

| Day | Task | OMEGA page |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Write version 1 of your plan (sections 1–3, 5) | Risk Guard |
| 2 | Fee, funding and liquidation calculations for 3 positions at 100 USDT | Futures, Positioning Desk |
| 3 | Lot and pip sizing for gold and one forex pair at your account size | Market Profiles |
| 4 | Full mark-up for 2 markets using the checklist | Analysis, Market Read |
| 5 | Mark-up again; compare yesterday's scenarios with what happened | Analysis, Journal |
| 6 | Sessions and calendar: convert this week's events to T&T time | — |
| 7 | **Weekly review #1** (process only — you've made no trades yet) | Journal |

## Week 2 — Paper trading with full risk rules (days 8–14)

| Day | Task | OMEGA page |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | Pre-market checklist + up to 2 paper trades, sized at 0.5% | Futures (paper), Journal |
| 9 | Same; record "setups not taken" too | Journal |
| 10 | Same; practise placing stop and exit orders at entry | Futures |
| 11 | Same; note emotion at entry for every trade | Journal |
| 12 | Same; compute R for each trade so far | Growth |
| 13 | Observe OMEGA Signals and CREED; log observed setups and outcomes | Signals, CREED |
| 14 | **Weekly review #2**: process score, rule breaks, one change | Journal, Growth |

Rules for week 2: maximum 2 trades a day, 0.5% risk, Risk Guard limits apply even on paper. If you hit the daily stop on paper, stop — you're practising the habit.

## Week 3 — Testing an idea (days 15–21)

| Day | Task | OMEGA page |
|---|---|---|
| 15 | Write a full test plan for one idea (Module 7 template); fingerprint it | — |
| 16 | Discovery: record every occurrence in the discovery period | Analysis / Research Lab |
| 17 | Luck check: same number of random entries | — |
| 18 | Validation: run once, record | — |
| 19 | Final: run once, record; write verdict with caveats | — |
| 20 | Research Lab: run or review one condition's in-sample vs held-out result | Research Lab |
| 21 | **Weekly review #3** + continue daily paper trades (max 1 a day this week) | Journal |

## Week 4 — Routine, automation and the plan (days 22–30)

| Day | Task | OMEGA page |
|---|---|---|
| 22 | Full routine: checklist → window → journal → 10-minute review | Command |
| 23 | Same, plus news rule practice around a scheduled event | — |
| 24 | Start (or review) a paper bot on a tested rule; find the kill switch | Trading Bots, Autopilot |
| 25 | Routine + paper trades | — |
| 26 | Write your tilt plan and stop-trading list | — |
| 27 | Routine + paper trades | — |
| 28 | Monthly check: expectancy (with how many trades), drawdown, process score | Growth, Scoreboard |
| 29 | Rewrite your plan as version 2 using everything you learned | — |
| 30 | **Capstone** (next lesson) | — |

## What "done" looks like after 30 days

- A written, dated trading plan (version 2).
- 20–40 paper trades logged with full fields, plus observed setups.
- One complete test of an idea, with an honest verdict.
- Four weekly reviews and one monthly check.
- A process score — for example "checklist used 26 of 30 days; 2 rule breaks".

You will **not** know whether you have an edge after 30 days. Nobody can, from 20–40 trades (Module 5: the uncertainty is too large). That's not the goal. The goal is a **process you can repeat** for the next 100–300 trades, at minimum risk, while the evidence builds.

## After the 30 days

- **Continue paper** until you have at least 50–100 trades of a setup with a positive label.
- **Move up the ladder** (paper → testnet → tiny live) only for setups with evidence.
- **Keep risk at the Risk Guard defaults or lower** for at least your first 100 live trades.
- **Re-read Modules 5 and 8** monthly. They're the ones people forget first.

## Exercise

1. Put the 30 days in your calendar with times.
2. Decide what you'll do on days you miss (catch up next day — don't double up).
3. Start Day 1 today.

lessons.title: Capstone: test, practise, review — and what comes next
lessons.body_md:
# Capstone

The capstone brings the whole course together in one project. When you finish it, you'll have done everything a careful trader does — on one idea, end to end, without risking money.

## The capstone brief

Choose **one** idea. It can be:

- an indicator rule you believed in before the course,
- a structure-based setup (for example a CREED-style pullback on one market),
- a session or volatility idea,
- or one of the passed setups observed through OMEGA Signals.

Then complete the six parts below and write a short report (1–2 pages).

### Part 1 — The plan (before any data)
Use the Module 7 template: hypothesis with a reason, exact entry and exit, costs, variants (and their number), periods, pass mark, luck check. Date it and save it before you look at results.

### Part 2 — The test
Run discovery, the luck check, validation (once) and final (once). Use a manual chart test or the Research Lab. Log every variant. Report results after costs, in R or %, with trade counts. Include results **without the best 5%** if you have enough trades, and the **worst single trade**.

### Part 3 — The verdict
PASS, FAIL or NOT ENOUGH TRADES — with at least two caveats. Label the setup (tested-pass, watch, untested, failed).

### Part 4 — Risk design
For your account size, write: risk per trade, position size for a typical stop (with the calculation), maximum leverage (and why — check the liquidation distance), daily/weekly stops, and what a normal losing streak would cost.

### Part 5 — Practice
Paper trade or observe the setup for at least **20 occurrences** (more if it's frequent), following your plan exactly. Log everything in the Journal: trades and setups not taken, emotion at entry, followed plan Y/N.

### Part 6 — Review
Compare your practice results with the test. Classify every loss (good loss / execution error / rule break / bad plan). Compute your process score. Decide: continue paper, move up the ladder, change one thing and re-test, or retire the idea.

## Report template

```
CAPSTONE REPORT                       Name ____  Date ____
Idea:
Plan written on:          Variants tried:
Discovery:   n __  mean __  t __    Random entries: mean __
Validation:  n __  mean __  t __
Final:       n __  mean __  t __    Without best 5%: __   Worst trade: __
Verdict + label:
Caveats (2+):
Risk design (size calc, leverage, limits):
Practice: n __  average R __  followed plan __/__  rule breaks __
Loss classification:
Decision and next step:
What I learned (3 lines):
```

## How to judge your own capstone

A **good** capstone is not one where the idea passed. Most ideas fail — in OMEGA's research, almost all did. A good capstone is one where:

- the plan was written before the data,
- every attempt was counted,
- costs were included,
- the verdict follows from the numbers,
- the risk design would survive a bad streak,
- the practice followed the plan, and
- the decision is honest.

A clean FAIL with good process is an excellent result. It just saved you real money.

## What you now know

Look back at where you started. You can now:

- explain spot, perps and CFDs, and calculate fees, funding, margin and liquidation at small account sizes;
- read a chart's structure, levels, volume and sessions without fooling yourself;
- use indicators as measuring tools, and explain why most indicator rules don't pay costs while volatility is predictable;
- size any trade, measure results in R, and design daily, weekly and review limits;
- explain exactly why 20× and 40× liquidated even the setups that passed;
- describe the climax reversal and panic bounce precisely — and why they're fading;
- use CREED as a discipline framework while knowing its measured coin-flip result;
- write and run a fair test with a luck check, and avoid the classic traps;
- run a daily routine, a journal and weekly reviews, and handle tilt and FOMO;
- climb the paper → testnet → live ladder with guards and a kill switch, and read a forward record.

## What comes next

1. **Keep the process going** for your next 100–300 trades, at minimum risk.
2. **Review monthly** against your plan and your retirement rules.
3. **Re-test** when markets change; edges fade.
4. **Stay sceptical** — of courses, signals, bots and your own best ideas. Including this course: check its claims against your own records.
5. **Course updates** will add new research results as OMEGA's forward records grow, including the forward-scored scouts and signals.

## A final word on risk

Trading can lose money quickly, and nothing in this course promises profit. If you trade, trade small, unleveraged, with money you can afford to lose, and only with methods that survived a fair test. The traders who last are not the ones with the best predictions; they are the ones who manage risk, test before they trust, and keep showing up with a plan.

## Exercise

Complete the capstone and fill in the report template. Save it with your trading plan. In three months, read both again — and write version 3 of your plan.

A clean FAIL with good process is an excellent result — it saved you real money.

Stay sceptical of everything — courses, signals, bots and your own best ideas.
